Investor Michael Burry states that stock indices are overstretched and warns investors to prepare for a potential 15- to 20-year span of low or negative real returns. He bases this assessment on historical market data, inflation metrics, and comparisons to three past market cycles.

Market Speculation and Overstretched Indices

Burry, writing in an X article on Oct. 18, noted that the S&P 500 reached a record high on Oct. 6 without significant trading volume. He contrasts the modern investing environment, where trades are free and information is ubiquitous, with the 1980s when stock quotes were found in newspapers and brokers charged high fees.

Today, Burry observes that the current market mantras are “Stonks go UP!” and “Buy the Dip, or BTFD.” However, he counters this optimism, stating, “Speculation has overrun investing, stock indices appear overstretched, and inflation is rearing its head again.” Consequently, he warns that “another 15-20 year period of negative or little real returns in stocks is in the offing.”

Read Also: Michael Burry Warns Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac Could Become ‘Worthless’ as Trump-Era Gains Collapse Under Fresh Pressure

Three Historical Bear Markets

While modern algorithmic traders excel at technical analysis, Burry notes that “what they do not generally do is history.” He outlines three prolonged periods of poor inflation-adjusted returns to demonstrate what a long-term bear market looks like.

From 1966 to 1982, the S&P 500’s inflation-adjusted price fell about 53%, excluding dividends. During the Great Depression era from 1929 to 1949, the real price return was negative 58%. More recently, from the 2000 market top through the 2011 trough, the S&P 500’s real price return was roughly negative 40%.

A ‘Very Long Wait’

Burry acknowledges that reinvesting dividends softens these declines. With dividends reinvested, the 1966 to 1982 loss shrinks to roughly 10%, the 2000 to 2011 loss drops to 25%, and a 1929 investor would be ahead by 1949.

However, he cautions that typical holding periods and life stages often prevent perfect dividend compounding. He concludes that “it has always been, one way or another, a very long wait rather than a wipeout for the patient holder through these three real bear markets.”

Billionaire entrepreneur Mark Cuban said on Sunday that U.S. manufacturing can come back if America catches up on robotics and software and stays ahead of China in artificial intelligence, responding to Anduril Industries co-founder Palmer Luckey’s case that American-made products are not impossible.

Our Robots Versus Their Robots

If the U.S. catches up on robotics and software, Cuban said in a post on X, “there is zero reason manufacturing won’t come back, or initiate here.”

He framed the contest with China as “Our Robots and AI vs their Robots and AI,” saying the U.S. must “stay ahead on AI.”

He pointed to his Cost Plus Drugs, where the only thing holding the company back from making generic drugs in Dallas for less than it can buy them from Asia is the fees it has to pay.

Read Also: Nasdaq Tumbles Over 2%, Records Weekly Loss: Investor Sentiment Weakens, Fear & Greed Index Moves to ‘Extreme Fear’ Zone

Manufacturing at Home Is Not Impossible

Luckey said that stories about iPhones costing $37,000 or laptops costing $100,000 are psychological operations, “sometimes pushed by foreign adversaries but more commonly by American corporations that want anything but an upset to the status quo.”

He added that companies that treat U.S. manufacturing as impossible want to justify staying in China and avoid admitting “it is a choice.”

A 30% tariff can bring production home only if it costs less than 30% more to produce in the U.S., Luckey said.

China Presses Ahead

Nvidia Corp. (NASDAQ:NVDA) held 34% of China’s AI accelerator market in the first half of 2026, while Huawei Technologies reached 28%, according to IDC, Reuters reported. Nvidia’s shipments fell 44%.

Memory chipmakers face growing competition from China, where ChangXin Memory Technologies reported progress on a denser DRAM design and plans server-memory products using it by the end of 2026.

In September, President Donald Trump rejected the idea of a U.S.-China AI joint venture because it could mean “giving a lot of secrets” to Beijing.

“We’re leading by a lot,” he said, adding that “whoever wins super intelligence wins.”

Intel Corp. (NASDAQ:INTC) stock climbed about 4% in premarket trading Monday as a broader technology rally lifted semiconductor stocks ahead of the chipmaker’s Oct. 29 earnings report.

The gains extend Intel’s 140% rally in 2026 as the company pushes deeper into artificial intelligence and seeks to capitalize on manufacturing constraints at rival Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co. Ltd. (NYSE:TSM).

Nasdaq futures rose 1.11%, while S&P 500 futures gained 0.53%, signaling renewed investor appetite for technology stocks after last week’s selloff.

Intel Targets Advanced AI Workloads

Intel announced Monday that it has enabled day-0 support for Meta Platforms Inc.’s (NASDAQ:META) Muse Spark Open, an 816 billion-parameter AI model, across its Xeon processors and upcoming GPU D-series.

The company said it successfully tested the model on four GPU D-series cards, each offering 160 GB of memory. The air-cooled design allows deployment in conventional data centers, potentially reducing infrastructure complexity.

Meanwhile, Intel’s Xeon processors support the model through memory-efficient AI processing, allowing businesses to run workloads privately on existing infrastructure.

Meta’s Muse Spark Open focuses on coding, debugging and automated workflows. It also supports image, audio, video and document processing.

The development strengthens Intel’s push into enterprise AI infrastructure as demand grows for hardware capable of running increasingly complex models.

For Intel, the integration highlights its efforts to expand beyond traditional processors and compete for enterprise AI infrastructure spending.

However, the announcement did not disclose customer commitments, expected revenue or a commercial launch date for the GPU D-series.

Intel To Showcase Edge And Physical AI At Web Summit 2026

Separately, Intel will also showcase its edge AI, agentic AI and physical AI technologies at Web Summit 2026 in Lisbon, Portugal, from Nov. 9-12.

The company plans live demonstrations highlighting AI applications across manufacturing, smart cities, retail, robotics and healthcare.

Intel will focus on how its chips, software and industry partnerships can help businesses move AI projects from pilot programs to real-world deployment.

Intel experts will also discuss the challenges of scaling AI, including infrastructure costs, system integration, power efficiency, and deployment complexity.

Taiwan Semiconductor’s Capacity Constraints Could Benefit Intel

Meanwhile, Intel could benefit from tightening manufacturing and advanced-packaging capacity at Taiwan Semiconductor, as major chipmakers compete for limited AI chip supplies.

Mizuho Securities Managing Director Jordan Klein said Intel CEO Lip-Bu Tan is working to improve manufacturing execution and attract outside foundry customers.

The capacity crunch could encourage companies such as Apple Inc. (NASDAQ:AAPL) and NVIDIA Corp. (NASDAQ:NVDA) to explore Intel as an alternative manufacturing partner.

However, potential agreements remain speculative, and Intel must demonstrate reliable production capabilities to capitalize on the opportunity.

Intel Earnings Could Test Turnaround Momentum

Intel is scheduled to report third-quarter earnings on Thursday, Oct. 29.

Analysts expect earnings of 39 cents per share, up from 23 cents a year earlier.

Revenue is projected to rise to $16.44 billion from $13.65 billion in the year-ago quarter.

Investors will likely focus on Intel’s AI strategy, progress in advanced manufacturing and its ability to secure external foundry customers.

Top ETF Exposure

Intel carries a 6.47% weighting in the VanEck Semiconductor ETF (NASDAQ:SMH), 9.44% in the iShares Semiconductor ETF (NASDAQ:SOXX) and 7.26% in the MicroSectors FANG & Innovation 3x Leveraged ETN (NYSE:BULZ).

These exposures could amplify Intel’s sensitivity to semiconductor-sector fund flows, although the impact depends on fund activity and market conditions.

Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh stated that he failed to adequately focus on non-monetary policy functions, including bank supervision, during his first 148 days in office.

Warsh Admits Neglect

Speaking at a fireside chat with International Monetary Fund Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva during the IMF-World Bank Annual Meetings on Oct. 16, Warsh admitted that his initial tenure disproportionately favored monetary policy over other mandates.

“I’d say where I would say I’ve failed in my first 148 days is mostly because of all of you and the people that are on the end of this camera. They’re all focused on monetary policy,” Warsh stated.

Warsh highlighted that “75% of the people at the Federal Reserve” do not work directly on monetary policy, according to his remarks. Instead, these employees manage functions given to the central bank by Congress, including “supervision and regulation, payment systems, consumer and community affairs,” he said.

Read Also: Fed Chair Kevin Warsh Keeps October Rate Hike in Limbo, Warns AI Could Trigger a ‘Very Bumpy’ Transition: ‘No Free Riders’

Prioritizing Institutional Credibility

Warsh confessed that he had not communicated his support effectively to those operational divisions. “I haven’t been as good as I need to be to make sure they know I care about their issues everybody as much as I care about the conduct of monetary policy,” Warsh noted.

The Fed Chairman emphasized that “the head of the Fed needs to be the head of all parts of the Fed.” He warned that the central bank’s true power derives from its institutional credibility rather than just monetary tools.

“And so whatever any part of the Federal Reserve does, if they slip up, if they stumble on supervision or on payments, that reflects on our institutional credibility,” he explained.

The Next Hundred Days

To correct this imbalance, Warsh outlined a shift in his upcoming leadership agenda. “So my next hundred days I’m going to try to give equal focus those other parts of the business because they matter too,” he declared.

Warsh concluded that leading the central bank requires questioning the status quo across all departments. “When you take over a position like this you need to lead all of it and you need to love the institution enough across everything they do to go back and ask first principles instead of will we do it this way because that’s how we’ve always done it,” he stated.

Microsoft Corp. (NASDAQ:MSFT) has abandoned a U.K. data center deal with Nscale amid power constraints at the project site, exposing a growing obstacle to the rapid expansion of AI infrastructure.

Power Shortages Derail Microsoft Deal

Microsoft withdrew from Nscale’s planned data center in Loughton, Essex, amid uncertainty over electricity supply.

Reuters on Sunday cited the Telegraph as reporting that grid officials do not expect the site to receive power until the 2030s.

The Financial Times reported that Microsoft planned to lease the facility’s entire 50-megawatt capacity. The site was expected to house approximately 23,000 NVIDIA Corp. (NASDAQ:NVDA) GB300 chips as part of Microsoft’s broader U.K. AI investment.

Microsoft declined to comment to Bloomberg and Reuters.

Nscale Maintains Microsoft Partnership

Nscale said it remains committed to the project and is exploring alternative power sources and expansion sites.

The company also said its long-term relationship with Microsoft remains strong and that London’s grid constraints would not affect other contracts.

Bloomberg reported that Microsoft and Anthropic account for roughly 85% of Nscale’s contracts. However, the Financial Times said the Essex project represents a small portion of Microsoft’s overall business with Nscale.

IPO Plans Face Fresh Challenges

The setback comes as Nscale prepares for a potential IPO as early as this month, with the company seeking to raise up to $3 billion, according to Bloomberg.

The development follows mounting investor concerns over debt-funded AI infrastructure expansion.

CoreWeave Inc. (NASDAQ:CRWV) recently recorded its worst weekly performance since November amid financing concerns. Separately, Firmus abandoned its IPO after struggling to attract investors at its proposed valuation.

AI Expansion Faces Power and Funding Risks

The Financial Times reported that Nscale faces potential penalties if it misses data center delivery deadlines.

Anthropic could also exit a $45 billion agreement linked to Nscale’s West Virginia project if financing or delivery milestones are missed.

The developments highlight how power availability, funding and construction delays could slow AI infrastructure expansion despite strong demand for computing capacity.

Meta Platforms Inc. (NASDAQ:META) stock fell nearly 1% in Monday’s premarket trading, despite gains in broader technology stocks, as investors positioned themselves ahead of the company’s Oct. 21 earnings report.

Nasdaq futures climbed 1.33%, while S&P 500 futures rose 0.64%.

Earnings and AI Growth in Focus

Meta’s upcoming earnings report is drawing investor attention as traders assess advertising performance, AI investments and future growth prospects.

The stock has also pulled back after approaching its 52-week high. As a result, some investors may be taking profits ahead of the report.

Meanwhile, Meta’s expanding AI business is showing early promise, although questions remain about user engagement and monetization.

According to BNP Paribas senior analyst Nick Jones, Meta’s Muse AI app has surpassed 10.4 million downloads since its Sept. 8 launch. Downloads peaked on the 12th day before stabilizing through day 38.

Early U.S. downloads outpaced those of OpenAI’s ChatGPT and Sora, partly benefiting from Meta’s massive user base across Facebook, Instagram and WhatsApp.

However, Jones flagged a key challenge. Muse’s mobile app open rate has stabilized below those of ChatGPT, Google and Meta’s existing apps. Its 14-day user retention also trails ChatGPT, raising concerns about sustained engagement.

Additionally, adoption remains concentrated among male users, while younger consumers account for a relatively small share.

New AI Features Could Support Adoption

Despite these challenges, Jones sees opportunities for Meta to strengthen Muse’s appeal.

The company’s Oct. 12 launch of Muse Wonder could help attract more users. Although the technology primarily targets enterprises and developers, it will also power Muse, initially for paid subscribers.

Meta currently offers a free basic tier alongside paid subscriptions for higher usage. It also earns small transaction fees through partnerships.

However, long-term monetization remains uncertain. Advertising could eventually become a larger revenue opportunity if engagement improves.

Jones also highlighted competition from Alphabet Inc. (NASDAQ:GOOGL), xAI and OpenAI’s Dots platform, alongside potential privacy and security risks.

For now, BNP Paribas considers daily active users and retention critical measures of Muse’s progress. Steady downloads without corresponding growth in daily usage could signal the need for product improvements.

Nevertheless, Jones maintained a bullish outlook on Meta, with an $885 price forecast. That implies approximately 20% upside from the stock’s Oct. 15 price of $736.70.

The analyst expects Meta’s extensive social media ecosystem to support continued adoption, even as the company works to turn early interest into lasting engagement.

On July 6, President Donald Trump stood in the Oval Office before a wall of television cameras, flanked by executives from the New York Stock Exchange, Nasdaq and some of the country’s biggest technology companies.

The occasion was the launch of "Trump Accounts," a federal investment initiative for American children. As Trump described the program, he singled out a $6.25 billion contribution from the billionaire computer entrepreneur Michael Dell and his wife, Susan.

Then the president offered something that sounded less like a policy announcement and more like a commercial endorsement.

"Go out and buy a Dell computer."

Wall Street reacted almost immediately. Shares of Dell Technologies (NYSE:DELL) jumped as much as 9 percent in intraday trading after the president’s remarks.

To casual observers, it sounded like a classic, off-script Trump moment. But what the public could not see from the Oval Office was another fact: the president’s own investment accounts held millions of dollars in Dell stock.

A financial disclosure released by the U.S. Office of Government Ethics showed that accounts holding the president’s investments had purchased between $1 million and $5 million of Dell shares on Feb. 10. The disclosure showed extensive trading in Dell across multiple accounts over the preceding year.

And July wasn’t the first time Trump had promoted the company.

Nine days after the February purchase, during a rally in Rome, Georgia, Trump urged the crowd to "go out and buy a Dell computer." He again recommended the company during a Mother’s Day event at the White House in May.

The overlap between Trump’s investments and his public endorsement of Dell was unusually conspicuous. But it wasn’t a one-off.

A Recurring Pattern

In a special collaboration with financial-data platform Unusual Whales, Benzinga examined Trump’s disclosed trades alongside public records, identifying a series of instances in which companies held in the president’s investment accounts were later publicly lauded by Trump, affected by administration policies or positioned to benefit from federal government business.

Unusual Whales compiled much of the trading data used in the analysis from federal financial disclosures.

Trump’s accounts recorded more than 21,000 securities transactions in 2025 alone, according to his annual financial disclosure released by the U.S. Office of Government Ethics in June 2026.

Trump’s accounts bought shares of Palantir Technologies (NASDAQ:PLTR) seven times in March, in transactions totaling between $247,000 and $630,000. On April 10, Trump hailed the defense-software company by name — and ticker symbol — on Truth Social, writing: "Palantir Technologies (PLTR) has proven to have great war fighting capabilities and equipment."

Palantir shares, which were on a downtrend in the preceding weeks, bottomed out that very day and climbed 3.4% the next day. The stock rallied almost 25 percent to an April 22 peak.

Between March 2 and March 23, Trump’s accounts accumulated between $217,000 and $530,000 in Micron (NASDAQ:MU) stock across four trades. On March 26, the president called into Fox News’ talk show The Five and publicly promoted the company following a meeting with Micron CEO Sanjay Mehrotra, stating: “I just left the head of Micron. It’s one of the hottest companies.”

Micron shares rose 0.5% the following day, before going on to surge 242 percent in the second quarter amid a much broader, AI-fueled boom in memory-chip demand and prices.

‘A National Security Disaster’

On Jan. 6, Trump’s accounts purchased between $500,000 and $1 million of NVIDIA Corporation (NASDAQ:NVDA) stock and between $50,000 and $100,000 of Advanced Micro Devices (NASDAQ:AMD). Seven days later, the Commerce Department formally revised its licensing policy for the chips, implementing a change the president had announced on Dec. 8, allowing the two chipmakers to resume selling certain artificial-intelligence chips to Chinese customers.

AMD’s stock jumped 6.4% the same day, extending the advance to 28% by Jan. 23.

The overlap drew further scrutiny when Trump brought Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang with him on a high-profile trip to China alongside other business leaders, including Elon Musk, Tim Cook and Larry Fink, as the president sought to advance U.S. business deals with Beijing.

Sen. Elizabeth Warren, Democrat of Massachusetts, seized on Huang’s inclusion after Trump’s Nvidia holdings became public.

"Trump brought the NVIDIA CEO on his trip to China to lobby Xi Jinping to buy advanced AI chips, even though it would create a U.S. national security threat," Warren wrote on X. "It turns out Trump also bought millions in NVIDIA’s stock. The President’s corruption is a national security disaster."

On Feb. 10 — the same day as the Dell purchase — Trump’s accounts bought between $1 million and $5 million in shares of Axon Enterprise (NASDAQ:AXON), the maker of Tasers and law-enforcement technology, as reported by CNBC. Fourteen days later, Immigration and Customs Enforcement posted a sources-sought notice outlining a potential five-year, $220 million purchase of roughly 17,800 conductive-energy weapons — more than quadrupling its existing inventory of about 4,300. The notice did not name Axon, but called for an upgrade to the "T10" and specifications that procurement reviewers and policing experts told CNBC effectively pointed to Axon’s TASER 10.

Axon shares surged almost 18% the very next day.

Unusual Whales highlighted the "unusual" proximity of Trump’s stock purchase to the public notice. The notice, however, was an early-stage request for information rather than a contract award, and federal procurement rules call for acquisition planning and market research to begin before such procurements are formally solicited. 

Those were not the only holdings to overlap with Trump’s public activity. Other companies in his portfolio that later received public support or exposure from the president included Tesla (NASDAQ:TSLA), Boeing (NYSE:BA), American Eagle (NYSE:AEO) and TKO Group Holdings (NYSE:TKO), whose UFC staged an event at the White House after Trump had purchased its shares.

The Conflict-of-Interest Question

None of those sequences, by itself, establishes that Trump ordered a trade, knew that one had been made or took an official action to increase the value of an investment. Nor does the timing alone establish a connection between a trade and a subsequent presidential statement, policy decision or government action.

Trump’s accounts have generated thousands of transactions across a broad portfolio, while decisions made by any president routinely affect large numbers of publicly traded companies. Some overlap, therefore, would be expected even in the absence of any impropriety.

The size of the individual positions also matters. Even purchases running into several million dollars represent only a small fraction of Trump’s overall fortune. Forbes estimated his net worth at about $6.7 billion as of Oct. 16, while a Reuters analysis of his financial disclosures put his traditional stock-and-bond holdings alone at between $703 million and $2.6 billion at the end of 2025.

The companies examined here therefore do not appear to represent a principal source of Trump’s wealth or recent income. His disclosures showed more than $1.4 billion in income from cryptocurrency ventures in 2025 alone, alongside substantial income from other businesses. The significance of the individual stock holdings is less their ability to transform Trump’s personal finances than the fact that they leave a sitting president with financial exposure — however small relative to his overall fortune — to individual companies whose fortunes can be affected by his words and government decisions.

Nor is a presidential endorsement, by itself, evidence of anything improper. Presidents routinely meet executives, praise American companies and promote businesses or industries they believe advance their economic agenda. Investors may also treat favorable comments from a president as commercially significant, producing a market reaction regardless of whether the president has any financial interest in the company.

Subsequent stock performance can be even harder to attribute. Share prices respond to earnings, industry trends, economic conditions and countless other factors. Micron’s extraordinary second-quarter rally, for example, unfolded amid a much broader boom in memory-chip demand and pricing tied to artificial-intelligence investment. And because Trump’s portfolio contains a large number of individual companies, some businesses he publicly discusses or whose industries benefit from administration policies would be expected to appear among his holdings without any improper connection.

The Remaining Issue

The issue examined here is therefore not whether a Trump endorsement caused a stock to rise, or whether ownership proves an endorsement was motivated by personal gain. It is the narrower question of what happens when a president retains financial exposure to individual companies while simultaneously possessing unusual power to promote them publicly or affect the environments in which they operate — a premise the White House rejects.

"As President Trump said, he has a lot of assets because he was a massively successful businessman prior to becoming President, which was why he was elected to office in the first place," White House Principal Deputy Press Secretary Anna Kelly told Benzinga in a statement.

"The President has implemented policies that have made all Americans wealthier and more prosperous – including cutting taxes, reshoring manufacturing, negotiating fairer trade deals, creating Trump Accounts for children, and more. All of the President’s assets are held in fully discretionary accounts managed by independent third-party financial institutions. There are no conflicts of interest," Kelly said.

For critics, however, the concern persists because of the breadth of presidential power over businesses in which Trump can remain financially exposed.

"Few things have eroded public trust in government as visibly as headlines about President Trump and his family getting rich from stock trading," Rep. Ro Khanna (D-Calif.) told Benzinga. "The American people deserve confidence that public office is not being used for private financial gain."

‘No Conflicts of Interest’

Trump and his representatives reject the premise that the investments present a conflict.

"I don’t get involved in my personal — we have funds that run my money," Trump told reporters when questioned about his investments earlier this year, according to CNBC.

He said he did not communicate with those managing the accounts.

"I don’t know what they call — closed accounts or something," Trump said. "You put your money in, and that’s it. I don’t talk to them, they’re big institutions, and they run it."

The White House offered Benzinga a more detailed version of that defense.

"All of the President’s assets are held in fully discretionary accounts managed by independent third-party financial institutions," Anna Kelly, the White House principal deputy press secretary, said in a statement. "There are no conflicts of interest."

Kelly also referred Benzinga to a social-media post on the matter from Eric Trump.

The president’s son has said that neither the president, his family nor the Trump Organization selects investments, receives advance notice of trades or can override the managers.

But to Richard Painter, a former chief White House ethics lawyer under President George W. Bush, the question extends beyond who clicked the button to buy the shares.

Painter has argued that even an executive-branch employee who owned no shares at all should not use public office to promote a particular company. After Trump’s Dell remarks, he said that "there should never be an endorsement of a particular company," according to Fortune.

Blind Trust or Not?

That lies at the center of the controversy.

The question is whether independent management resolves the conflict when a president remains financially exposed to companies whose fortunes he can affect.

Previous presidents generally took a different approach. George H.W. Bush, Bill Clinton and George W. Bush used blind trusts. Barack Obama held diversified mutual funds through a blind trust. Joe Biden made no individual stock trades while in the White House, according to his OGE financial disclosures, which show only a handful of fund transactions within an annuity.

The president’s son posted on X on May 15 that Trump family assets were also held in a blind trust: "All of our assets are invested in a blind trust by the largest financial institutions in broad market indexes."

However, the New York Times reported just days later that there were no signs such a trust existed, without saying how they obtained the information. The Trump Organization later said the investments are maintained exclusively in fully discretionary accounts managed by independent third-party brokerages, the media outlet added.

The Pelosi Problem

For Trump, the controversy carries an additional political complication: He has spent years arguing that elected officials should not be allowed to profit from stock trading — and has made Rep. Nancy Pelosi (D-Calif.) the most prominent target of that campaign.

In his 2026 State of the Union address, Trump called on Congress to prohibit lawmakers from trading stocks, framing the issue as one of public corruption.

"As we ensure that all Americans can profit from a rising stock market, let’s also make sure that members of Congress cannot corruptly profit from using insider information," Trump told lawmakers.

Then he singled out Pelosi, whose husband, Paul Pelosi, has made large investments in technology companies through stocks and options.

"Pass the Stop Insider Trading Act without delay," Trump said.

The appeal drew bipartisan applause. Pelosi has become the most recognizable symbol of congressional stock trading, though she and her husband have maintained that he makes his investment decisions independently and without inside information from her office.

That defense has an obvious resemblance to the argument Trump’s representatives make about his own portfolio: Someone else makes the investment decisions.

Calls for a Broader Ban

Khanna, who has pushed for restrictions on congressional trading for years, told Benzinga that the principle should extend to the White House.

Khanna himself has faced scrutiny over his household’s investment performance. Investor Anthony Pompliano once labeled him the "new king" of congressional stock trading after sharing data on his reported returns. Khanna has rejected that characterization, saying he neither owns nor trades stocks himself.

"My household’s only investments are in a trust that my in-laws set up before my marriage, managed independently by a third party in full compliance with Office of Government Ethics rules," Khanna previously told Benzinga.

Pompliano, who has publicly criticized congressional stock trading, has not made a comparable public comment on Trump’s disclosed stock activity.

Benzinga sought comment from Pompliano for this article but did not receive a response.

Khanna said the same principle should apply across the government. "I have spent years working to tackle corruption in government, and I do not believe the President or his family should be trading stocks while in office," he said. "I also do not believe members of Congress should be trading stocks either."

Some Republicans have reached the same conclusion.

In May, Sen. Josh Hawley (R-Mo.) said he favored a prohibition that would apply broadly across government.

"I’d be in favor of a uniform rule for everybody," Hawley told NBC News after being asked about Trump’s stock trades. "By everybody, I mean everybody, Supreme Court justices, you pick it, that says you can’t trade in stock."

Trump pushed back.

"I don’t think real Republicans want to see their President, who has had unprecedented success, TARGETED," he wrote on Truth Social, calling Hawley a "second-tier Senator."

Hawley later said there had been a misunderstanding over how the proposal would affect Trump. The legislation was subsequently structured so that elected officials already in office, including Trump, would not have to stop trading until the beginning of their next term.

Rep. Marlin Stutzman, (R-Ind.), also said in May that all three branches of government should be subjected to a stock-trading ban "sooner rather than later."

Trump Excluded From House Bill

But when a congressional trading bill finally reached the House floor in July, the sitting president was not covered by it.

H.R. 7008, which passed 232 to 198, would bar members of Congress, their spouses and dependent children from making new individual-stock purchases while allowing them to retain existing holdings and sell them with seven to 14 days’ public notice. Diversified funds and commodities would remain permitted, and the bill placed no comparable restriction on Trump or other executive branch officials.

Republicans defending the legislation argued that forcing lawmakers to divest existing investments could discourage successful businesspeople from entering public service.

"What we want to do is make sure we’re not locking out people who come from a successful business," Sen. Pete Ricketts (R-Neb.), said.

But the stock-trading measure did not reach the floor as standalone legislation. Republicans had attached voter-identification provisions mirroring elements of the SAVE America Act, tying the stock-trading restrictions to a separate and politically contentious fight over election rules. 

"Breaking: 198 Democrats just voted against the Stop Insider Trading Act, which bans members of Congress from trading stocks while in office. Shameful," the White House posted on X.

The post received a Community Note explaining that the legislation also contained voter-ID provisions and that Democrats had opposed the combined bill.

Critics Challenge the House Bill

Rep. Thomas Massie, (R-Ky.), had warned before the vote that attaching voter ID would produce exactly that political dynamic. Republicans added the provision, he wrote on X, not to win Democratic support but "to get them to vote against the stock trading ban, so they can use it in the Nov. election."

Massie and Trump were already at odds on a range of issues, including federal spending and foreign policy. Trump had backed a primary challenger who defeated Massie in May after a bitter campaign.

Massie called instead for stand-alone legislation.

The framing nevertheless spread beyond Washington. Billionaire investor Bill Ackman was among those who questioned how Democrats could vote against the Stop Insider Trading Act. After the Nancy Pelosi Tracker account responded by pointing to Trump’s exclusion and the addition of the voter-ID provisions, Ackman deleted his post.

Democratic lawmakers, meanwhile, attacked not only the voter-ID addition but the substance of the trading restrictions themselves.

Rep. Joseph Morelle (D-New York) accused Republicans of having "corrupted their so-called stock trading bill" by attaching part of the SAVE America Act, as reported by Politico.

Rep. Jim McGovern (D-Mass.) was more explicit.

In an X post, he called it a "watered-down bill" and "a bandaid on a bullet hole," arguing that it barred lawmakers from buying stocks but still allowed them to sell existing holdings.

‘The Biggest Stock Trader’

Rep. James Clyburn (D-S.C.) likewise said he opposed the measure because lawmakers could still own and sell stocks while it excluded "the biggest stock trader in our government — the President of the United States."

Rep. Sean Casten (D-Ill.) brought the criticism directly back to the scale of Trump’s activity.

"The bill does not apply to Donald Trump who, in the last year, traded more stocks than ALL MEMBERS OF CONGRESS COMBINED," Casten wrote. "It is not a serious piece of legislation."

The fight exposed a broader inconsistency in Washington’s stock-trading debate: Congress has spent years wrestling with whether lawmakers should own companies whose fortunes they can influence through public office.

The president possesses powers that can reach even further.

Trump Tracker’s Temporary Suspension

That breadth of presidential power is what caught the attention of the anonymous creator of the Donald Trump Portfolio Tracker, an X account launched in July to catalog the president’s disclosed investments and the government actions surrounding them.

The creator told Benzinga the account began as a personal effort to make sense of Trump’s disclosures before unexpectedly attracting a large audience. 

The account has since amassed more than 170,000 followers.

The rapid rise also brought scrutiny of its own. The account was suspended by X for several days on the grounds that it was an "inauthentic account." The creator told Benzinga that an appeal was initially denied. The account was reinstated only after other users began drawing attention to the suspension and posts about the ban went viral.

The episode does not establish that the suspension was politically motivated. But it brought additional attention to both the account and the scrutiny it was directing at the president’s financial activity. 

The creator said the disclosures did not prove insider trading, but revealed what he called "ownership overlapping with authority" — a president investing in companies while exercising power over policies, contracts and regulatory decisions that can affect them.

The creator said Trump’s disclosed investments span industries touched directly by federal policy, including defense, surveillance, semiconductors, energy, health care and insurance.

Some of the potential conflicts are less about a single presidential statement or government contract than about the direction of an entire administration.

The tracker pointed, for instance, to Trump’s holdings in private-prison operators GEO Group (NYSE:GEO) and CoreCivic (NYSE:CXW), companies positioned to benefit from the administration’s expansion of immigration detention and enforcement. It also highlighted Trump’s large financial interest in Trump Media & Technology Group (NASDAQ:DJT), whose stock can move with developments in the president’s own political fortunes.

‘A Nine-Figure Position’

"A sitting president holding a nine-figure position in a stock that moves on his own fortunes is genuinely without precedent," the tracker’s creator said.

The White House says independent management eliminates any conflict. The tracker’s creator disagrees. 

"Discretionary isn’t blind, and disclosure isn’t divestment," the creator said.

Independent management still leaves the president financially exposed to companies he can praise, regulate, contract with or otherwise influence.

Trump himself has argued that such financial entanglements can undermine confidence in public office. At the State of the Union, he called for an end to congressional stock trading and invoked Pelosi as the example of what Washington should no longer tolerate.

For the creator of the Trump Portfolio Tracker, that leaves a question the president’s own argument has made difficult to avoid.

"If trading on policy information is corrupt for a member of Congress," the creator said, "it’s hard to explain why holding — and actively trading — the entire universe of companies you regulate is fine for the president."

The United States government recorded a budget deficit of $1.992 trillion for fiscal year 2026, with federal interest payments exceeding defense spending. Moody’s Analytics Chief Economist Mark Zandi stated this trajectory moves the country toward a “fiscal reckoning.”

Budget and Outlay Data

The Treasury Department reported that the $1.992 trillion deficit for the period ending Sept. 30 resulted from $7.396 trillion in total outlays and $5.403 trillion in total receipts. Zandi noted the deficit represents more than 6% of the Gross Domestic Product. The government spent $1.052 trillion on net interest during the fiscal year. This outpaced the $965 billion spent on national defense.

The primary budget deficit, which excludes interest payments, reached nearly 3% of GDP. Zandi called this figure “eye-popping.” He stated that because unemployment remains low, the primary budget should be in surplus or balanced. He attributed the $1 trillion in interest payments to the “ballooning debt load.”

Read Also: BlackRock CEO Larry Fink Says $40 Trillion US Debt ‘Will Not Be as Consequential’ If AI Drives 3% GDP Growth

Treasury Yields and Market Reaction

Zandi observed that global investors “appear to be demanding a higher rate to compensate for the mounting risk.” The 10-year Treasury yield rose by about one percentage point this year. Zandi stated this increase is among the largest of any major economy. He noted that nations with the heaviest interest burdens experienced the biggest yield increases.

Cycle of Debt

Zandi cautioned that a “vicious cycle threatens to take hold” within the economy. He explained that higher rates add to the debt load and interest payments, which subsequently pushes rates higher.

He acknowledged that other countries face similar issues, but he emphasized the U.S. is the most important because U.S. Treasuries act as the global benchmark.

How Have the Bond and Stock Markets Performed?

At the last check, the 30-year Treasury bond yielded 5.41%, the 10-year Treasury bond was at 5.07%, and the two-year bond was at 4.73%.

The primary ETF specifically tracking the long end of the U.S. Treasury yield curve—including the 30-year benchmark bond—is the iShares 20+ Year Treasury Bond ETF (NASDAQ:TLT), which closed 0.10% higher at $80.05 on Friday. It was down 8.89% year-to-date, down 1.03% over the last month and 12.36% over the last year.

The S&P 500 index has advanced 11.68% year-to-date. Similarly, the Nasdaq Composite index was up 12.50%, and the Dow Jones gained 7.48% YTD.

On Friday, the SPDR S&P 500 ETF Trust (NYSE:SPY) and Invesco QQQ Trust ETF (NASDAQ:QQQ), which track the S&P 500 and Nasdaq-100, respectively, closed lower. SPY fell 1.11% to $763.25, while QQQ declined 2.50% to $709.80. Meanwhile, the Dow tracker, State Street SPDR Dow Jones Industrial Average ETF Trust (NYSE:DIA), ended 0.38% lower at $519.10.

In premarket trading on Monday, SPY was up 0.64%, QQQ rose 1.30%, and DIA advanced by 0.027%.

Nebius Group N.V. (NASDAQ:NBIS) stock rose more than 6% in Monday’s premarket trading, rebounding after a roughly 25% decline last week.

The recovery followed renewed analyst support and improved sentiment toward technology stocks.

Nasdaq futures climbed 1.16%, while S&P 500 futures gained 0.45%, providing a favorable backdrop for AI infrastructure stocks.

However, Nebius shares remain below several key moving averages, suggesting that selling pressure has yet to subside.

Truist Maintains Bullish Outlook

On Sunday, Truist reiterated its Buy rating on Nebius, with a $355 price forecast.

The firm argued that concerns following the failed Firmus initial public offering do not necessarily indicate broader weakness among neocloud providers with substantial contracted backlogs.

The outlook offers a counterpoint to investor concerns over rising financing costs, debt burdens and the capital-intensive nature of AI infrastructure expansion.

See More: Top Value Stocks

Neoclouds Face Growing Competitive Pressure

Still, competition remains a concern for smaller AI cloud providers.

Silvant Capital Management’s Michael Sansoterra warned that neocloud companies face an uphill battle against technology giants with stronger balance sheets, established customer relationships and extensive infrastructure.

He told CNBC Friday that companies such as CoreWeave Inc. (NASDAQ:CRWV) must compete with hyperscalers that have significant financial and operational advantages.

Sansoterra expects the largest cloud providers to capture most of the economic profits from AI spending. However, he acknowledged that some neocloud companies could still generate attractive investment returns.

For Nebius, strong AI demand and contracted revenue offer growth opportunities. Nevertheless, heavy financing requirements and intensifying competition could pressure future profitability.

Nebius remains under short-term pressure despite Monday’s rebound.

The stock trades 20.6% below its 20-day simple moving average (SMA) and 20.3% below its 50-day SMA. However, it remains roughly 2% above its 200-day SMA, suggesting the longer-term trend has not fully broken down.

A sustained recovery could face resistance near $220, where several moving averages converge.

PayPal Holdings Inc. (NASDAQ:PYPL) stock is trending as renewed takeover speculation draws attention to an unconfirmed report from September that an unnamed West Coast tech company may be evaluating an all-stock deal for the company.

  • PayPal stock is under selling pressure. Why are PYPL shares declining?

A September Betaville Alert Pointed to an Unnamed West Coast Tech Company and an All-Stock Deal

On Sept. 25, traders circulated a Betaville "uncooked" alert, or early and unverified deal chatter, that an unnamed West Coast U.S. technology company may be weighing an all-stock takeover of PayPal, according to Seeking Alpha. No buyer was named, PayPal did not confirm an approach, and the board is said to prefer cash. Shares rose that day.

Retail Traders Guess Meta but Are Split on Whether a Bid Is Real

According to Stocktwits, renewed takeover speculation is driving attention to the stock, with many traders guessing Meta Platforms Inc. (NASDAQ:META) as the possible buyer. No offer or buyer has been confirmed. The community is split between expecting a premium bid and viewing the rumor as a short-lived pump, while some focus on PayPal’s standalone turnaround and upcoming earnings.

The Rumor Follows Stripe and Advent’s Abandoned $53 Billion Bid

In July, Stripe and Advent International offered about $60.50 a share, or roughly $53 billion, a premium of about 28% to PayPal’s mid-July price. Talks continued into August, then collapsed in late August after the board viewed the price as too low and the two sides clashed over structure, including a reported $2 billion breakup fee. Shares fell about 13% in a day when the bid died. CEO Enrique Lores, who took over in March, has said PayPal will weigh outside offers against its standalone plan, which includes cost cuts and a large share-repurchase program. Bernstein analysts estimated PayPal’s board would want an offer meaningfully above $70 a share, according to Yahoo Finance.

PayPal Reports Third-Quarter Results Oct. 27

PayPal is set to report earnings on Oct. 27 before the market opens. Analysts estimate earnings per share of $1.31 and revenue of $8.71 billion. PayPal guided to a low-single-digit decline in third-quarter earnings per share, about $1.30 to $1.33 on a normalized basis, and has raised its full-year non-GAAP earnings per share outlook to about $5.38.

Investors keep selling chip stocks. The iShares Semiconductor ETF (NASDAQ:SOXX) fell 11.8% last week. It has now declined for nine straight days—its longest losing streak since 2006.

The damage was worse among the companies that build chipmaking machines and memory. Applied Materials Inc. (NASDAQ:AMAT) fell 19.3%, Lam Research Corp. (NASDAQ:LRCX) dropped 17.2% and Micron Technology Inc. (NASDAQ:MU) lost 14.6%.

The fear behind the selling had a simple shape. The artificial intelligence boom might be running out of buyers.

Online, that fear had already found its own words. Searches for "companies reducing artificial intelligence spending" surged on Google Trends, after a wave of reports on corporations cutting back on AI tools.

If companies spend less on AI, the reasoning goes, chipmakers will sell less.

Yet research notes that Wall Street analysts in the past few days say the opposite.

Bank Of America Sees A Cycle Priced For A Crash

Bank of America analyst Vivek Arya said in a Friday note that the chip sector already prices in a collapse he does not expect.

AI leaders Nvidia Corp. (NASDAQ:NVDA), Broadcom Inc. (NASDAQ:AVGO) and Micron trade at about 13 times forward earnings on average, according to Arya.

That multiple compares a stock’s price with the profit analysts expect over the next 12 months.

It sits within the range Cisco Systems Inc. (NASDAQ:CSCO) traded at after the dot-com bubble burst.

"Investors are paying post-crash multiples for a cycle that hasn’t crashed," Arya said.

The comparison with 2000 also breaks down on usage.

Back then, telecom companies had laid fiber-optic cable that sat idle. Today’s AI infrastructure runs near full utilization, according to Arya.

Prices back that up.

Rental rates for Nvidia’s older graphics processors, launched in 2020, 2022 and 2024, are up between 12% and 37% this year.

For Arya, that points to scarcity rather than oversupply.

Bank of America also estimates capital spending by the large cloud providers and specialist AI clouds at about $1.01 trillion in 2026, up 98% from last year. It sees about $1.39 trillion in 2027.

Read Also: Nvidia, Micron and Broadcom Already Trade Like Cisco Post Dot-Com Burst: Bank of America

Cantor’s C.J. Muse Says Equipment Is Sold Out

On Monday, Cantor Fitzgerald analyst C.J. Muse published his team’s takeaways from the SemiconWest trade show in San Francisco.

The first point directly addressed last week’s fear.

The analysts said chip equipment "is effectively sold out," with customers giving at least eight quarters of visibility.

ASML Holding NV (NASDAQ:ASML) is receiving purchase orders for 2029 and 2030, according to the note.

Applied Materials is tracking 110 new chip plants.

Micron expects memory supply to be even tighter in 2027 than in 2026, with customers holding little to no inventory.

Muse also described frustration among management teams. Most are operating in the strongest backdrop they have ever seen, while their share prices fall, according to the note.

“We continue to recommend remaining Overweight Semis, as we view today’s AI Infrastructure buildout as durable and elongated,” the analyst said.

Why Companies Reducing AI Spending Is The Wrong Signal

Oxford Economics raised its outlook for global business technology spending growth in 2026 to 14.8%, from 11.4%, in an Oct. 6 report.

Spending on AI-related products is set to top $510 billion this year, up 54%, as firms move from experimentation towards operational deployment, according to the firm.

“Global AI-related spending is projected to reach $3.4 trillion by 2035, or 23% of tech spend,” , Oxford Economics said.

The Real Risk Ahead Is AI Monetization

None of this makes the AI trade risk-free. Bank of America’s equity and quant strategy team led by Savita Subramanian pointed to a different problem in a separate Friday note.

AI capital spending has beaten forecasts by about 50% this year, while AI revenue has beaten them by only about 20%, according to the strategists. Meanwhile, the cost of capital for the largest cloud providers has risen to about 10%, up from 4% in 2023.

In other words, every dollar of data-center spending now has to earn more to pay for itself.

For the strategists, "monetization vs. cost of capital is the only question that matters."

Bitcoin (CRYPTO: BTC) could eventually reach a $50 trillion valuation, macro investor Jordi Visser says, as hedge funds unwind leverage while Bitcoin quietly outperforms every major asset class.

Why Visser Says Hedge Funds Are Blowing Up, Not AI

Visser said on Anthony Pompliano‘s podcast Saturday that the market selloff tied to AI stocks has nothing to do with AI itself failing.

He compared it instead to 1998’s Long-Term Capital Management collapse, arguing leveraged hedge funds, not the AI buildout, are the real source of stress.

His evidence: Lone Pine Capital was up more than 40% through September before giving back the entire gain, proof in Visser’s view that something structural is breaking in how funds use leverage rather than any flaw in AI’s growth story.

Visser also pushed back on dot-com comparisons for AI infrastructure companies.

CoreWeave (NASDAQ:CRWV), he said, differs fundamentally from that era since its revenue comes from Microsoft (NASDAQ:MSFT), Meta (NASDAQ:META) and OpenAI rather than speculative telecom debt. 

He argued AI’s eventual earnings remain inevitable because demand for compute keeps outpacing supply, even when individual stock valuations overshoot in the short term.

Why Bitcoin Keeps Holding While Everything Else Wobbles

Visser said Bitcoin has traded between $82,000 and $85,000 for four months while the S&P 500 (NYSE:SPY) and Nasdaq sat flat and bonds declined, a sign he reads as Bitcoin acting as a safe landing spot as capital flees riskier, leveraged trades. 

He called this “good Sharpe ratio” behavior standing out precisely because so few other assets are generating clean returns right now.

Asked whether Bitcoin could realistically reach a $50 trillion valuation, Visser said “of course it could,” pointing to roughly $900 trillion in largely illiquid global assets that tokenization could eventually unlock into liquid, tradable form. 

He argued the same logic applies to Bitcoin that Elon Musk has floated for SpaceX (NASDAQ:SPCX): as a much larger pool of capital turns liquid, a single asset’s value can scale right alongside it.

Why Visser Flags November and December as Key Windows

Visser said he expects the next major move higher in both AI stocks and Bitcoin to come around two specific windows: right after hyperscaler earnings reports later this month, and again in December, when many funds stop taking risk for the year. 

He noted that AI-linked long-short positioning on Morgan Stanley’s (NYSE:MS) prime brokerage desk has fallen to the seventh percentile of the past year, suggesting most leveraged risk has already been pulled from the trade.

He downplayed September’s hotter-than-expected CPI print entirely, arguing that inflation readings between 2% and 3.5% have little bearing on markets unless they coincide with actual job losses, which he said remain near historic lows.

Five years ago, on October 14, I launched TKer, the newsletter that tells the story of how the stock market usually goes up.

That first year was highlighted by a bear market as the Federal Reserve went to war against inflation. The S&P 500 fell 19%.

Year two brought an impressive stock market rebound. It began two days after the current bull market started. That year, the S&P ended up 21% higher despite lingering uncertainty.

Year three extended the rally, with the S&P surging an incredible 35%. Interestingly, the average annualized return since TKer’s launch up to that point was an extraordinarily average 9%.

Year four brought political upheaval after the U.S. presidential election, trade wars sparked by new tariffs, volatility in interest rates and currency markets, heightened geopolitical tensions, threats to Federal Reserve independence, and a government shutdown, which added to concerns about the quality of economic data. Yet the stock market repeatedly set new all-time highs, climbing 14% during the period — arguably because earnings were resilient.

📈 Year five saw many of year four’s challenges linger. But one key difference was that the forward price-to-earnings (P/E) ratio was unusually elevated at close to 23x, the highest level since 2020.

In other words, stocks looked expensive when I published my previous annual update.

But as we’ve discussed for years, elevated valuations don’t mean prices are likely to fall soon. We were reminded of this in TKer’s fifth year as the S&P 500 climbed 16%.

TKer Stock Market Truth No. 6 📜

About a year ago, some of Wall Street’s most prominent strategists made a bold prediction: High valuations were justified, and they’ll remain elevated in 2026 as stock prices go higher.

Others argued valuations were a headwind and at risk of contracting, capping price returns.

I’ve written before that P/E ratio forecasts are where Wall Street’s year-end price target calculations often go wrong, mostly because the direction of the ratio is hard to predict over short periods.

But ten months into 2026, P/E ratios have been contracting. Does that mean the bulls were wrong and the skeptics were right?

Sort of, but also not really.

One of this year’s defining market stories has been the aggressive, ongoing upward revisions to earnings forecasts, which have pulled P/E ratios down. This occurred even as stock prices trended higher. Fractions 101: If the denominator (E) rises faster than the numerator (P), then the P/E falls.

This brings us to TKer Stock Market Truth No. 6:

6. Valuations won’t tell you much about next year

There are many valuation methods that’ll help you estimate whether a stock or stock market is cheap or expensive. We won’t go through all of those here.

While valuation methods may tell you something about long-term returns, most tell you almost nothing about where prices are headed in the next 12 months. Over short periods like this, expensive things can get more expensive and cheap things can get cheaper.

It’s worth noting that prices can be cheap or expensive for extended periods of time. In fact, some folks would argue valuations are not mean-reverting.

Expensive stocks often get more expensive. Cheap stocks often get cheaper.

And sometimes prices fall as stocks get more expensive, and prices rise as they get cheaper.

Trading the stock market can be hard. You could’ve been absolutely right if you predicted P/E ratios would contract. But if you used that information to sell stocks, you might’ve made a huge mistake.

Prices for specialized optical fiber used inside AI data centers are forecast to average more than five times their 2025 levels this year.

That could be good news for Corning Incorporated (NYSE:GLW), a major manufacturer of fiber-optic cables and connectivity equipment. The company has a supply agreement worth up to $6 billion with Meta Platforms Inc. (NASDAQ:META).

Corning’s Optical Communications business is already booming. Second-quarter sales jumped 32% to $2.07 billion, while segment net income surged 77% to $438 million.

But CEO Wendell Weeks says higher fiber prices aren’t the main reason.

Why Higher Fiber Prices Aren’t the Whole Story

TrendForce released new research Monday forecasting a global optical fiber shortage of 180 million fiber-kilometers this year, with shortages potentially lasting until 2028.

TrendForce puts industry capacity utilization at 92%, while inventories have fallen to just one month’s supply. Expanding production typically takes 18 to 24 months.

As fiber supplies tighten, major customers are signing long-term agreements to secure future deliveries.

Corning’s agreement with Meta runs through 2030 and covers fiber, cables and connectivity products. Meta will also serve as the main customer for an expansion of Corning’s North Carolina cable factory, giving the manufacturer committed demand as it increases production.

During July’s earnings call, Wolfe Research analyst George Notter questioned Weeks about rising prices and the company’s growing reliance on long-term agreements.

“The price is higher, but that really isn’t how we’re driving that profitability improvement,” Weeks said.

Instead, Weeks credited higher-value connectivity products that help customers build networks faster and more cheaply.

Weeks added that Corning could sell more of its newest products if it had the capacity to manufacture them.

Wall Street Remains Bullish Despite Selloff

Corning shares have lost roughly half their value since hitting a record high in June, despite booming demand for its optical products.

UBS raised its price target for Corning to $201 earlier this month, maintaining a Buy rating. Citi is even more bullish, with a $220 target, while Bernstein is more cautious at $140.

On Polymarket, traders put roughly 28% odds on Corning’s third-quarter optical revenue exceeding $2.3 billion, although trading volume is just $3,500.

Meanwhile, a separate Polymarket puts roughly 9% odds on an AI industry downturn meeting the contract’s specific conditions by year-end, with more than $3 million traded on the market.

Meta reports earnings Wednesday, Oct. 21, followed by Corning on Oct. 27.

Walmart Inc. (NYSE:WMT) could unlock billions of dollars in advertising revenue as it expands its digital advertising business, strengthens its connected TV presence and integrates artificial intelligence into shopping, according to Bank of America.

Bank of America analyst Christopher Nardone maintained a Buy rating on Walmart with a $126 price forecast on Monday.

Advertising Business Gains Momentum

Following a meeting with Walmart Connect executive Ryan Mayward, Nardone highlighted the retailer’s growing ability to attract advertising dollars from competing platforms.

Walmart’s access to roughly 150 million weekly shoppers gives advertisers valuable consumer insights and helps the company measure advertising effectiveness.

Meanwhile, Walmart continues to add tens of thousands of third-party marketplace sellers, creating another source of advertising revenue.

Bank of America estimates that marketplace sellers typically spend 10% to 12% of gross merchandise value on advertising, compared with 4% to 6% for traditional Walmart suppliers.

Connected TV Opens Multibillion-Dollar Opportunity

The analyst also highlighted Walmart’s acquisitions of Vizio in December 2024 and Vibe.co in August 2026.

These deals expand Walmart’s reach beyond brands selling products through its stores and marketplace.

Vibe’s self-service platform allows small and midsize businesses to launch and measure streaming TV campaigns using Walmart’s consumer data.

Nardone believes these advertisers could represent a multibillion-dollar opportunity over the longer term.

Walmart’s investment in Vizio’s WatchFree+ streaming service also provides additional advertising inventory.

See More: Top Value Stocks

AI Shopping and Sam’s Club Offer More Growth

Bank of America sees Walmart as a potential beneficiary of AI-powered shopping because of its integrations with multiple AI platforms.

The retailer operates its own AI shopping assistant, Sparky, and has partnered with external platforms, including Meta Platforms, Inc.’s (NASDAQ:META) Muse.

However, the analyst cautioned that it remains too early to determine how AI shopping agents will reshape advertising.

Meanwhile, Walmart is moving Sam’s Club’s U.S. advertising operations onto Walmart’s technology platform. The integration could encourage brands to increase advertising spending across Walmart, Sam’s Club and international markets.

Valuation and Risks

Bank of America’s $126 price forecast reflects 40 times its fiscal 2028 adjusted earnings estimate, above Walmart’s average forward earnings multiple of 36 over the past two years.

The premium reflects expectations for continued market share gains, stronger store traffic and operating income growth approaching twice the pace of sales growth.

However, the firm identified slowing food inflation, tougher competition and weaker global retail conditions as potential risks to its outlook.

Roche Holdings AG (OTC:RHHBY) Germany chief Daniel Steiners announced that the Swiss pharmaceutical giant has put all future investment decisions in Germany on hold.

The Swiss drug maker argues that recent government healthcare austerity requirements have shattered corporate trust and undermined long-term planning for the pharmaceutical sector.

Mandatory Rebates Erode Industry Confidence

Steiners voiced sharp opposition to the GKV Contribution Rate Stabilization Act, which increases statutory manufacturer discounts on patent-protected drugs from 7% to 15.5% starting in January 2027.

Read Also: Roche Secures FDA Approval for First At-Home Thyroid Eye Disease Therapy

While Germany’s health ministry expects the measure to save health insurers around 12 billion euros by 2030 to help bridge an estimated 19 billion euros financing shortfall, Steiners warned that such short-term austerity ignores structural financing issues and risks driving research and production abroad.

Steiners also dismissed Berlin’s proposed location clause—which offers partial rebate relief to companies with extensive domestic research and manufacturing—as inadequate.

He insisted that piecemeal adjustments cannot replace a comprehensive industrial strategy, contrasting Germany’s tightening regulatory climate with the U.S., where supportive policies and infrastructure assistance actively attract life sciences capital.

Setback For Merz’s Economic Pitch

The investment freeze delivers a direct blow to German Chancellor Friedrich Merz, who is actively pitching the country to global executives at a Berlin investor summit.

Financial Times noted in August that Roche is not alone in pulling back; U.S.-based drugmaker Eli Lilly and Co. (NYSE:LLY) recently halved a planned 2.3 billion euros manufacturing investment, while Pfizer Inc. (NYSE:PFE) placed its domestic allocations under review and Boehringer Ingelheim scrapped a 900 million euros expenditure.

Statutory health insurance officials strongly defended the government’s reforms. Stefanie Stoff-Ahnis, deputy chairwoman of the GKV association, maintained that pharmaceutical companies continue to enjoy substantial profits in Germany, cautioning that higher drug prices would destabilize recently balanced insurance finances without offering tangible benefits to patients.

Roche employs around 18,600 people in Germany and has poured approximately 3.8 billion euros into expanding its domestic sites since 2020.

A company spokeswoman told FT that the freeze applies exclusively to unapproved future projects, ensuring that ongoing construction at its Penzberg biotechnology hub and current workforce headcounts remain secure for now.

Roche Expands China-Based Partnership

On the other hand, on Monday, Hansoh Pharmaceutical Group Co., Ltd. announced a second collaboration with Roche in the antibody-drug conjugate (ADC) field.

The strategic collaboration spans a broad portfolio of ADC programs, comprising two preclinical Hansoh ADC programs and multiple ADC programs based on Roche-proposed targets powered by Hansoh’s proprietary ADC technology platform.

Under the collaboration agreement, Hansoh will lead the early development of the programs up to the completion of global PhaseⅠa clinical trials.

Roche will be responsible for further developing the programs worldwide (excluding the Chinese Mainland, Hong Kong, Macau and Taiwan). Hansoh will retain all rights to develop, register and commercialize the programs within the Chinese Mainland, Hong Kong, Macau and Taiwan.

Hansoh will receive an upfront payment of $400 million as well as a first anniversary payment of $110 million, and will be eligible to receive potentially more than $15 billion in milestone payments.

In April 2020, with most of America locked indoors, the country’s home builders recorded their darkest mood in eight years.

Six years later, with no virus and no lockdown, they feel even worse.

The NAHB/Wells Fargo Housing Market Index (HMI), a monthly survey tracking builder confidence in the market for newly built single-family homes, fell three points to 29 in October.

That is the lowest reading since June 2012, below the 30 recorded in April 2020, and short of the 32 economists expected.

All three components of the main index fell.

Current sales conditions dropped two points to 33, sales expectations for the next six months slid five points to 32, and prospective buyer traffic plunged five points to 18.

The main trigger is the cost of money.

The 30-year fixed mortgage rate averaged 7.40% last week, the highest in nearly three years, according to Freddie Mac.

"Mortgage rates have climbed well above 7% in recent weeks, and higher gas prices and inflation have further weakened buyer traffic across much of the country," NAHB Chairman Bill Owens said.

Chart: Homebuilder Sentiment Sinks Below 2020 Lows, Hitting June 2012 Levels

Builders Are Paying To Keep Buyers

To keep sales moving, builders are giving up margin. In October, 43% of builders cut prices, the highest share during the 2020-2026 period, according to NAHB.

The average cut held at 6% for a seventh straight month.

Meanwhile, 65% of builders used sales incentives, such as mortgage rate buydowns.

It was the 19th straight month that at least 60% of builders have done so.

Labor is a second pressure point. More than one-third of builders reported immigration enforcement activity in their market areas in the past month, according to Owens, causing construction delays.

"Housing remains squeezed by supply-side constraints and significant affordability challenges," NAHB Chief Economist Robert Dietz said.

"Demand persists, but higher mortgage rates, elevated construction costs and weaker consumer confidence are keeping more buyers on the sidelines," he added.

Economists See Little Relief Ahead

Pantheon Macroeconomics’ Oliver Allen said the typical 30-year mortgage rate has jumped to around 7.5%, from roughly 6.6% in early July.

He warned that "if anything—confidence is likely to fall much further over the next month or two, given the recent trends in rates."

Oxford Economics cut its forecasts for housing starts, home sales and home price growth on Monday.

"A median-income household now earns less than three-quarters of what it needs to afford a median-priced home, and the rise in rates this year alone has put homeownership out of reach for another 5 million households," Lead US Economist Nancy Vanden Houten said.

"We don’t expect a meaningful improvement in housing activity until around the end of 2027, when we look for mortgage rates to decline," she added.

XHB/SPY: Back To Pandemic Levels

Wall Street has priced the slowdown in for months.

The SPDR S&P Homebuilders ETF (NYSE:XHB) relative to the SPDR S&P 500 ETF Trust (NYSE:SPY) traded at 0.1229 Monday.

That’s slightly above last week’s lows, but the ratio remains at levels last seen during the pandemic crisis.

On Oct. 14, it closed at 0.1206, its lowest level since April 2020.

At its late-September 2024 peak, the same ratio was close to 0.218. Builders have lost roughly 43% of their value relative to the S&P 500 in two years.

Over that stretch, XHB is down 24% while SPY has gained 34%.

This year, the homebuilder ETF is down almost 9% while the S&P 500 tracker is up nearly 12%.

Why Homebuilders Could Become An AI Hedge

One scenario could change that quickly, and it has little to do with housing.

22V Research analyst Dennis DeBusschere said in a Friday note that the artificial intelligence investment boom has crowded out housing.

"Real Private Residential Fixed investment has not contributed to GDP in 4 years as private fixed investment (AI capex) has accelerated," DeBusschere said.

In his view, consumer spending and AI capital spending have pushed U.S. growth well above trend. That has kept 10-year yields high, and high yields are what keep buyers away from new homes.

The logic also works in reverse.

Housing would contribute to economic growth if AI capex suddenly fell. The Fed would cut rates aggressively and 10-year yields would decline, DeBusschere said.

"Long Homebuilders is an interesting AI capex decline hedge,” he added.

More than 24 gigawatts of data center capacity is already in advanced construction across just 40 campuses, most of it expected to come online in 2027, according to new research from SemiAnalysis.

The research firm forecasts 50 gigawatts of new data center capacity outside China in 2027, roughly as much as the industry had built in those markets over its entire history up to the end of 2024.

The bullish outlook comes as Microsoft Corp. (NASDAQ:MSFT) walked away from a U.K. data center agreement because of electricity delays. The 50-megawatt facility was expected to house approximately 23,000 Nvidia Corp. (NASDAQ:NVDA) GB300 chips.

Why SemiAnalysis Expects the Boom to Continue

Most of the 40 campuses are more than halfway completed, with cooling and electrical equipment already installed.

The researchers wrote that “gigantic sites are simply getting built, and many are on time” in Monday’s report.

Their confidence rests on a surge in long-term leases. Developers typically spend only 5% to 10% of a project’s budget before securing a customer, using signed contracts to raise financing.

SemiAnalysis estimates roughly $1 trillion in multiyear data center leases have been signed this year, helping fund construction scheduled for 2027 and 2028.

The firm also argues that “the power generation problem has broadly been solved.”

Rather than waiting five to 10 years for grid connections, developers are increasingly installing their own electricity generation, including fuel cells, refurbished turbines and engines originally designed for trucks.

These alternatives could bypass the kind of grid delays that derailed Microsoft’s Essex deal, although they may not be practical at every location.

Construction is accelerating, too. SemiAnalysis says Singapore-based DayOne has cut building timelines from more than 18 months to around nine. The firm estimates that modular construction can reduce certain on-site labor requirements by up to 63%.

Could Chips Become the Next Bottleneck?

Not everyone shares SemiAnalysis’s optimism.

Altimeter Capital founder Brad Gerstner challenged an earlier 43-gigawatt projection from SemiAnalysis founder Dylan Patel on the All-In podcast.

“I would suggest Dylan’s forecast of 43 gigawatts next year is too aggressive,” Gerstner said, estimating actual delivery closer to 25 gigawatts. His comments focused on U.S. infrastructure, while SemiAnalysis’s latest forecast covers a broader market.

Meanwhile, traders on Polymarket put roughly 9% odds on an AI industry downturn by Dec. 31. The contract requires three qualifying events within 90 days, potentially including a 50% drop in Nvidia shares from their all-time high.

SemiAnalysis expects memory and processor shortages to become a bigger constraint in 2027 and 2028.

For Nvidia, that could mean demand for its chips continues to outstrip supply even as developers overcome the construction and electricity problems holding up projects today.
